2) The end-user license agreement is a legally binding document. This wasn't something they just hastily created and placed on the front page; it was crafted by legal professionals for the explicit purpose of protecting their interests. While the sale of digital games and audio occurs, an account as part of an online-only experience remains the property of the game creators, because at no point do you actually own a license to hold a copy of the game, as you do with other digital media; you rent an account, or in the case of certain games, they allow you to use one for free as long as they're okay with you using it.

3) In-game currency has no financial exchange value. In other words, once you own the currency, you have no right or ability to trade it back. The currency itself has a value, but only between yourself and the game developer. In the same way that a coupon you have for a discount at a restaurant is worth that discount, but in real terms, the coupon is not classified as having a financial value.

Because my position on art is that it does not exist as an abstract, it exists as a product of the mind that created it.

There are theories of art that suggest that artists don't create art, but more discover it, like a mathematician would discover a function or formula; that art exists in some way independently of the one who crafted it.

This isn't a theory of art I subscribe to. Instead, I feel that art is intrinsically linked to its creator. We can freely discuss the concepts that a piece of art can prompt us to conceive, those things that people ascribe as their interpretation, but those concepts prompted by the piece are something that exists because of yourself, not something intrinsic to the piece, because the piece itself was created with intent.

We can also freely discuss the artist's intent, and how well we feel the piece conveys that and what we feel they did to convey that and what else they could have done, in the form of critiquing the work. But this can only be done on the basis of assessing the work on its original design criteria and premise; something we can either attempt to discern ourselves, if we have no artist to check with, or something we can do if the artist confirms themselves what they were trying to convey.

But my point is these are two SEPARATE ways of analyzing and discussing art. We shouldn't conflate the interpretations we have of unrelated topics thanks to the influence of the piece, with some internal message of the piece itself.

In other words, the perspective of the audience is not invalid, but when discussing what art means, the positions are distinct from each other; one is internal to yourself, how the art makes you feel and think, and what the art does to bring that about within you, and another is abstract, based on what we think the message placed within a constructed piece is.

If you believe art to be a product of its creator, then that message is intrinsically linked to the artist, their wills and desires, whether conscious or not.

This is generally done because there is a much higher risk of complications in conjoined twins who aren't separated, but separation almost inevitably goes ahead regardless. I'd say the bigger issue in this situation is often the question of whose body it is. Genetically, those twins are, except in the rarest of rare cases, identical.

The majority of non-identical cases end up as chimerism, in that one fetus absorbs the other in utero, and potentially ends up with clusters of their cells in their body.

For the identical ones, there's generally some level of greater integration of the shared body parts to one body over another, but they are, technically, a single human body comprised of two persons. They're actually really interesting cases that muddy the waters a bit, but for the purposes of this debate, I'd say that if sufficient evidence could show which twin was medically dominant over the shared body part, that twin would have the right to have their twin removed. Not an easy decision to make by any means, but ethically justifiable.

In regards to the severed arm, for me personally it comes back to my original point about potential life; the fetus isn't currently an independent life, and therefore doesn't deserve rights independent of its mother. However, it has a potential for independent life that a severed limb does not. It is that potential future that makes us place greater importance on the fetus.

When it comes to the fusion issue, I'd again have to refer back to the twins' assessment; if there was good medical evidence to support whose body it was, I believe they do have a right to separate themselves, even if it results in the death of the other person.

Others may hold that humanity has no intrinsic value, but that personhood is what gives our lives value, and that until a life form can exist independently of the vital systems of its host, that life form lacks an independent right to exist.
